title: The Cell at Dar al-Shafa to the Torn Shroud: exile, the guardianship of the jurist, and a state made from a garden outside Paris
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Khomein, the birth in the cleric's house
stops.date_confidence: contested: the surviving birth certificate gives 17 May 1900; his brother and Iranian official biography give 24 September 1902. The pool prints both and resolves neither; the two dates yield 89 and 86 for the age at death.
stops.campa: In a house in the small town of Khomein, in the province of Markazi, a son is born to Sayyid Mostafa Musavi, the town's cleric, and his wife. They name him Ruhollah, Spirit of God. The family wears the black turban of descent from the Prophet and lives on its land and on the judgments the father gives. Two dates are entered against the birth by people entitled to know: the certificate says one thing, the family another, and the Islamic Republic he founds will keep the family's. The house survives him and is kept as a museum of the childhood.
suggested_refs: The preserved birth house at Khomein, kept as a museum of the childhood
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah (2000)

stops.name: Khomein, the father killed on the road
stops.date_confidence: contested and month unknown: Wikipedia says the boy was about two, giving 1903; Moin says five months after the birth. The exact site is not pinpointed by any source in the pool beyond the vicinity of the town.
stops.campa: Sayyid Mostafa is shot dead near Khomein at the order of a local landowner. One account puts the killing five months after the birth, another when the boy is about two; the ground it happened on is recorded only as somewhere outside the town. Ruhollah is raised afterward in a house of women, by his mother and his aunt, on the income of the family's land and the authority of the dead man's name. He is not old enough to remember his father, and the house he grows up in speaks of the killing as a martyrdom.
suggested_refs: The unlocated site of Sayyid Mostafa Musavi's killing, outside Khomein
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Arak, the seminary of Haeri Yazdi
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: At about twenty he goes north to Arak, called Sultanabad then, to enter the seminary that Sheikh Abdolkarim Haeri Yazdi has newly founded there. He studies logic, Arabic grammar, and the roots of jurisprudence among students drawn from every province of the country. It lasts about two years. Haeri accepts the invitation of the clergy of Qom to move his school to the shrine city, and the students follow their teacher across the desert road. The move that fixes where he will spend the next forty years of his life is his teacher's decision, taken for reasons of his teacher's own.
suggested_refs: Haeri Yazdi's seminary at Sultanabad, the first formal school

segments.name: Qom: Forty Years in the Seminary

stops.name: Qom, the cell at Dar al-Shafa
stops.date_confidence: contested year: the chronology lens gives 1921 for the transfer, the geography lens 1922. Same event, the move of Haeri's school to Qom. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes a cell in the Dar al-Shafa school beside the shrine of Fatima Masumeh, sister of the eighth Imam, and Qom becomes his address for forty years. He reads law and the roots of law, and then, past the ordinary syllabus, philosophy and the theoretical mysticism of Ibn Arabi, subjects the more literal jurists of the city regard as a contamination. He prays and teaches in the shrine precincts across those decades, which is a description of a habit rather than a record of a day. He is known first as a philosopher, which in Qom is not an unmixed compliment.
stops.quote: Only God, the Exalted, is the light; everything else is darkness.
stops.quote_source: Ruhollah Khomeini, Pithy Aphorisms: Wise Saying and Counsels, ed. Mansoor Limba (Tehran: Institute for Compilation and Publication of Imam Khomeini's Works), p. 3
suggested_refs: The Dar al-Shafa school and the shrine of Fatima Masumeh, Qom
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Qom, the commentary on the dawn supplication
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: His first book is not political. Sharh Du'a al-Sahar is a commentary on the supplication recited before dawn in Ramadan, written in the vocabulary of the mystics: light and darkness, the veil, the annihilation of the self before the divine names. He is twenty-eight, or twenty-six, according to which birth year is granted him. Nothing in it announces a state or a party. Sixty years later the Republic he founds will print his mystical verse and his rulings on jurisprudence in the same collected edition, and its readers will argue about which of the two came first in the man.
suggested_refs: Sharh Du'a al-Sahar, the first published work, 1928

stops.name: Tehran, the marriage to Khadijeh Saqafi
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only. No reachable biography names the house or venue; Tehran is recorded solely as the bride's family city, so the pin is a city, not a place.
stops.campa: He marries Khadijeh Saqafi, daughter of a Tehran cleric, in a match arranged between clerical houses. No biography within reach names the street or the room where the contract is read; the city is recorded because the bride's family lives in it. Seven children follow, among them Mostafa, Zahra, Farideh, and Ahmad. He is by then a teacher in Qom under the first Pahlavi shah, whose police are measuring turbans and forbidding the clerical cloak in the street. The marriage joins two families whose standing rests on the thing the state has begun to legislate against.
suggested_refs: The unrecorded Tehran house of the Saqafi family, 1929
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Mecca, the hajj without a date
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source fixes a year. The geography lens tags the pilgrimage [R] with the range circa 1930s-40s and states it rests on the expectation attaching to a scholar of his standing, not on a record. 1935 is a placeholder inside that range.
stops.campa: Tradition places him at the House of God in these decades, circling the black stone as an observant scholar of his standing is expected to do at least once. No biography fixes the year, and the journey survives only as an assumption about a life of that shape. The Algerian emir Abdelkader made this same circuit twice, at seventeen with his father and again as an old man with his war lost. Half a century after Khomeini's own pilgrimage, Iranian marchers will carry his portrait through these streets and more than four hundred people will die in the answer.
suggested_refs: The Masjid al-Haram at Mecca, undated in every reachable biography
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah (general reference to Hajj practice; tagged R in the pool)

stops.name: Qom, the Uncovering of Secrets
stops.date_confidence: contested year: chronology lens 1942, geography lens 1943, same book and same description. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He publishes Kashf al-Asrar, the Uncovering of Secrets, an answer to a pamphlet attacking the clergy and, through it, an attack on the secularizing state that Reza Shah built. It is his first work of political theology: the clergy have a right to be heard on government, and the monarchy holds no warrant of its own. He does not yet demand that the jurists rule. That argument will take another twenty-seven years and a rented house in Najaf. He is past forty, a teacher of ethics with a following of students and no public office of any kind.
stops.quote: There are hundreds of other [Koranic] psalms and hadiths urging Muslims to value war and to fight.
stops.quote_source: Ruhollah Khomeini, 'Islam Is Not a Religion of Pacifists' (1942), quoted in Barry Rubin and Judith Colp Rubin, Anti-American Terrorism and the Middle East (OUP, 2002)
suggested_refs: Kashf al-Asrar, first printing, Qom
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Qom, the rank of marja and the declaration
stops.date_confidence: the declaration is attested to 22 January 1963. The rise to marja on the death of Grand Ayatollah Borujerdi is dated 1963 by the chronology lens; no other lens carries that year and the pool offers no independent check on it.
stops.campa: With the death of Grand Ayatollah Borujerdi the Shia world holds no single source of emulation, and Khomeini rises among the men to whom the faithful may now turn. He uses the standing at once. On the twenty-second of January he issues a declaration against the Shah's White Revolution: land redistribution that will break the religious endowments, votes for women, an oath sworn on a book that is not the Quran, and behind all of it the hand of the United States. The Shah answers by calling the clergy black reaction. The declaration is read aloud from pulpits.
suggested_refs: The 22 January 1963 declaration against the White Revolution

stops.name: Qom, the paratroopers in the Feyziyeh
stops.date_confidence: corrected on verification: the geography lens dated the raid to January 1963, conflating it with the 26 January White Revolution referendum. The raid is 22 March 1963, the death anniversary of Ja'far al-Sadiq, with Nowruz still running.
stops.campa: On the death anniversary of Imam Jafar al-Sadiq, with the Nowruz holiday still in the courtyards, security forces and paratroopers enter the Feyziyeh madrasa and beat the students inside their own school. Some are thrown from the upper galleries. Khomeini refuses the customary silence of mourning and preaches instead, naming the government as the author of it. The school where he has taught for thirty years becomes the date the movement counts from, and he stops speaking about reforms and starts speaking about the man on the throne.
suggested_refs: The Feyziyeh madrasa at Qom, stormed 22 March 1963

stops.name: Qom, the sermon on the day of Ashura
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the tenth of Muharram, the day Hussain died at Karbala, he preaches in the Feyziyeh to a crowd that has come for the mourning. He addresses the Shah directly, warns him that the people will not grieve when he goes, and sets him beside Yazid, the caliph who killed the Prophet's grandson. In the Shia calendar no heavier charge is available to a speaker. The sermon is written down and copied and carried across the country. Two days later the government answers it by sending men to his house before dawn.
suggested_refs: The Ashura sermon of 3 June 1963 at the Feyziyeh

stops.name: Qom, the arrest at dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Agents take him from his house before dawn on the fifteenth of Khordad and drive him to Tehran. By morning the news is in the bazaars. Crowds come out in Qom, Tehran, Mashhad, and Shiraz, unarmed and refusing to disperse, and the army fires into them for three days; the dead are counted in the hundreds by the government and far higher by the opposition. The date becomes the name of the uprising. Every anniversary of it will be kept by the state he founds sixteen years later, and the dead of those three days will be counted as its first martyrs.
suggested_refs: The 15 Khordad uprising, 5-7 June 1963

stops.name: Tehran, Qasr Prison and the ten months
stops.date_confidence: corrected on verification: the chronology lens said he was released in August 1963. In August 1963 he was moved from the cells into house arrest in Tehran; he was not freed until 7 April 1964. Coordinates corrected from 35.7345, 51.4488, about 1.2 km north of the site.
stops.campa: He is held in Qasr Prison, the old Qajar garden turned penitentiary, and he is not tried; the government has worked out what a trial would make of him. In August he is moved out of the cells into house arrest at a guarded residence on the edge of the city, and there he stays through the winter, silenced by arrangement rather than by argument, while the movement outside acquires its martyrs and its date. He is released on the seventh of April 1964, after roughly ten months, and goes back to Qom to say the same things again.
suggested_refs: Qasr Prison, Tehran, now the Qasr Prison Museum
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Qom, the sermon on the capitulation
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Majlis has passed a law granting American military personnel in Iran immunity from Iranian courts, and an American loan follows it within days. Khomeini preaches on it in Qom. An American cook, he says, an American mechanic, may now kill an Iranian and answer to no Iranian judge; they have sold us. The sermon is printed and passed hand to hand across the country. Where the White Revolution had divided the clergy from the throne, this divides the nation from it, and the government concludes that he cannot remain inside the borders.
suggested_refs: The capitulation law of October 1964 and the sermon against it

segments.name: Bursa and Najaf: The Thirteen Years

stops.name: Bursa, the house of Colonel Ali Cetiner
stops.date_confidence: corrected on verification: deported 4 November 1964, but flown first to Ankara and moved to Bursa about a week later, c. 12 November. The chronology lens had him in Bursa on the day of the deportation.
stops.campa: Soldiers take him from his house on the fourth of November and fly him to Ankara; about a week later he is moved to Bursa and lodged in the home of a Turkish intelligence officer, Colonel Ali Cetiner, under watch. Republican Turkey forbids him the turban and the clerical robe in the street, and forbids him to preach at all. He reads and writes and waits out the winter. A hundred and eleven years earlier the Ottoman sultan settled another defeated exile of another Muslim war in this same city, the emir Abdelkader, on a pension paid by the government that had beaten him.
stops.quote: That which admits man to God's Threshold is his separation from all that is not of God, a thing which is not attainable by all.
stops.quote_source: Ruhollah Khomeini, Pithy Aphorisms: Wise Saying and Counsels, ed. Mansoor Limba (Tehran: Institute for Compilation and Publication of Imam Khomeini's Works), p. 4
suggested_refs: The house of Colonel Ali Cetiner at Bursa, the first exile

stops.name: Najaf, the house behind the golden dome
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; day defaulted to 01. Coordinates unified on the geography lens value; the afterlife lens value 32.0286, 44.3489 was corrected as about 3.7 km northeast of the shrine district.
stops.campa: After eleven months Turkey releases him and he settles in Najaf, in the lanes behind the golden dome where the first Imam is buried, the oldest teaching city of Shia Islam. He lives there thirteen years on the charity of followers, in a house of no distinction. Ibn Battuta walked these same lanes in the fourteenth century and wrote down the lamps and the silver of the shrine for people who would never see it. The senior clerics of Najaf keep their distance from politics and from him. He teaches anyway, and his students carry what he says back over the border.
suggested_refs: The exile house near the Imam Ali Shrine, Najaf, 1965-1978
sources: ibn_battuta.journey.json (geography only; Khomeini is not named in that file)

stops.name: Najaf, the lectures on the guardianship of the jurist
stops.date_confidence: the chronology and geography lenses give 1970; the afterlife lens gives 'around 1969-1970'. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Over a series of lectures to his students he argues that in the absence of the Hidden Imam the government of Islam belongs to the jurists who know the law; that monarchy is illegitimate in itself; that the clergy who confine themselves to ritual have abandoned their office. The lectures are transcribed as Hokumat-e Eslami, Islamic Government, and go into Iran as pamphlets and as cassette tape. The doctrine now has a name, velayat-e faqih. In nine years it will be the opening architecture of a constitution.
stops.quote: Anyone who will say that religion is separate from politics is a fool; he does not know Islam or politics.
stops.quote_source: Attributed; reproduced on Wikiquote, 'Ruhollah Khomeini', and not traced by the researcher to a primary publication. Tagged [R].
suggested_refs: Hokumat-e Eslami: Velayat-e Faqih, translated by Hamid Algar in Islam and Revolution (Mizan Press, 1981)
sources: Hamid Algar, trans., Islam and Revolution (1981)

stops.name: Karbala, the ground of Hussain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the geography lens tags the Karbala visits [R] for the range 1965-1978 and states that no source among the available biographies dates a particular visit. 1972 is a placeholder inside the exile years.
stops.campa: Fifty miles north of Najaf lies the ground where Hussain was killed, and the road between the two shrines is the ordinary circuit of every cleric in Iraq. Tradition places him on it. No biography dates a visit, and the stop stands on the custom of the country rather than on a record of a day. He has already used this ground as an argument: the Shah is Yazid, the people are Hussain's, and the killing of the Prophet's grandson is not an event of the year 680 but a description of the present. Standing here, the argument stops being a figure of speech.
suggested_refs: The Imam Hussain Shrine at Karbala, undated in the biographies
sources: General Najaf-Karbala clerical circuit; tagged R in the pool and not dated in Moin or Iranica

stops.name: Baghdad, the days to leave
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Shah asks Baghdad to silence him, and Saddam Hussein, then vice president and courting Tehran, agrees. Najaf goes under surveillance and then Khomeini is given days to be out of the country. He passes through Baghdad on his way out of a place he has lived thirteen years. Two years later the same man will send an army across the Iranian border, and the war that follows will run eight years and end with Khomeini saying he has drunk poison. The expulsion is the first move in it, made by a government trying to do a favour for a throne that has two months left.
suggested_refs: The Iraqi expulsion order of autumn 1978
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah
QUEUE.md line 224 (Saddam Hussein crossing, queue entry only)

stops.name: The Kuwait frontier, refused
stops.date_confidence: the pool dates the refusal to October 1978 without a day; 3 October is placed between the Baghdad expulsion and the 6 October arrival in France.
stops.campa: He drives south to the Kuwaiti border with his son Ahmad and asks to be let in. Kuwait, forewarned from Tehran, refuses him. He waits at the crossing, an old man with no country willing to receive him, and turns back. Then someone proposes France, where a tourist visa asks nothing of a foreign cleric and no government wants a quarrel over one. The choice that will put him in front of the cameras of the world is made at a frontier post by men counting the days they have left in Iraq, out of whatever is still available to them.
suggested_refs: The Iraq-Kuwait crossing where entry was refused, October 1978

stops.name: Paris, the landing at Orly
stops.date_confidence: attested. Note the two-day gap with the Neauphle house, occupied from 8 October 1978; no source in the pool reconciles them.
stops.campa: He lands in France on a tourist visa. The government considers deporting him, decides an elderly cleric is not worth the trouble, and lets him stay on condition that he abstain from political activity, a condition nobody troubles to enforce. He has come from a shrine city where his audience was students and pilgrims to a country where his audience is the international press. In thirteen years in Najaf almost no photograph of him circulated in the West. In the next four months he is on the front page of everything.
suggested_refs: The French tourist visa of October 1978

stops.name: Neauphle-le-Chateau, the garden under the apple tree
stops.date_confidence: the house at 67 Route de Chevreuse was occupied from 8 October 1978. Four different coordinates for the village appear in the pool; this pin is inherited byte-identical from michel_foucault.journey.json.
stops.campa: Iranian exiles rent a house for him in Neauphle-le-Chateau, a village west of Paris, and a second house across the road for the journalists. He sits on a carpet in the garden under an apple tree and receives the correspondents of the world, one after another, month after month, answering in sentences short enough to survive translation. Telephone lines run to Tehran and what he says in the garden is on cassette in the bazaar within a day. He commands no army and holds no office, and the state that will replace the monarchy is planned from this garden.
suggested_refs: The house at 67 Route de Chevreuse, Neauphle-le-Chateau, since demolished
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Paris, the cassettes and the philosopher
stops.date_confidence: representative date for the autumn 1978 tape traffic; the canonical Paris pin is inherited byte-identical from michel_foucault.journey.json, which treats the region as inheriting the Neauphle geography.
stops.campa: The revolution moves by cassette: sermons recorded in the garden, flown to Tehran, copied in back rooms, played from the loudspeakers of mosques to people who have never seen his face. In these same weeks Michel Foucault comes back from Tehran, where he walked in the demonstrations for the Corriere della Sera and went down to Qom to sit with the clerics, and writes that he has seen a political spirituality, a thing Europe lost in the sixteenth century. The two men are in one metropolitan region and no meeting is recorded. Foucault spends years afterward answering for the sentence.
suggested_refs: Foucault's autumn 1978 Corriere della Sera dispatches from Tehran and Qom
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Tehran, the Shah leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi flies out of Mehrabad saying he is going abroad for a rest. The newspaper headline is two words. In the streets people knock the heads from his statues and hold the front pages above them like placards. The throne he is leaving was saved for him once already, in 1953, when a coup run by the American and British services removed Mohammad Mosaddegh and brought back a monarch who had fled the country days before. It has taken twenty-six years for the second flight, and there is no service now willing to reverse it.
suggested_refs: The departure of Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, 16 January 1979

stops.name: Tehran, the landing at Mehrabad
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Air France charter comes down at Mehrabad after fifteen years and three months of exile. The road into the city is lined the whole way; the crowd is put at several million and no count is possible. On the aircraft an American correspondent, Peter Jennings, asks him what he feels on returning to Iran after so long. He answers with one word, and it goes around the world, and it is read as ice, as mysticism, as contempt, and as the plain statement of a man who holds that what he feels is not the subject.
stops.quote_source: Reply to ABC News correspondent Peter Jennings on the flight to Tehran, 1 February 1979; reported translation: Nothing. English Wikipedia, 'Ruhollah Khomeini', n. 90
suggested_refs: The Air France charter of 1 February 1979 and the Jennings exchange

stops.name: Behesht-e Zahra, the speech over the graves
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates corrected on verification: the geography lens gave 35.5686, 51.4381, about 7 km east of the cemetery; the longitude was the error.
stops.campa: He is driven from the airport not to a mosque but to the cemetery, to the section where the dead of the past year's street fighting are buried, and he speaks standing among their graves. He declares the government of Shapour Bakhtiar, which the Shah appointed and the Majlis approved, to be nothing: the nation has not chosen it, therefore it is not a government. He says he will appoint one himself. It is a claim of sovereignty made by a private person standing on a burial ground, and within ten days it is true.
stops.quote: I shall kick their teeth in. I appoint the government.
stops.quote_source: On Shapour Bakhtiar's provisional government, February 1979; English Wikipedia, 'Ruhollah Khomeini', nn. 96-97, attributing it to contemporary press and biographical accounts
suggested_refs: The Behesht-e Zahra address of 1 February 1979
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Tehran, the Refah School
stops.date_confidence: corrected on verification: the chronology lens dated the Bazargan appointment 11 February 1979; the correct date is 4 February. The quotes lens still dates the accompanying line to 11 February, and that discrepancy is left standing. The coordinates are the geography lens's own approximation, tagged [R] there.
stops.campa: He sets up in the Refah School, an Islamic girls' school in Tehran, and governs out of its classrooms: a revolutionary council in one room, a queue of officers coming to change sides in another. On the fourth of February he appoints Mehdi Bazargan, an engineer and a liberal of the old National Front, prime minister of a provisional government, and tells the crowd that since he has appointed him he must be obeyed. The country now has two prime ministers, and only one of them has soldiers who will still fire.
stops.quote: since I have appointed him, he must be obeyed
stops.quote_source: On the appointment of Mehdi Bazargan as interim prime minister; English Wikipedia, 'Ruhollah Khomeini', n. 98, which dates the line 11 February 1979
suggested_refs: The Refah School, Tehran, headquarters of the revolution in February 1979

stops.name: Tehran, the monarchy ends
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: After two days of fighting between air force cadets and the Imperial Guard, the army declares itself neutral and the Pahlavi state stops existing. Bakhtiar goes into hiding and then into exile. In the streets the crowds chant a slogan that is nobody's quotation, neither East nor West, Islamic Republic, and within a year it is the published foreign policy of a country. Khomeini, in Iran ten days, tells them the revolution will not stop at this border. The throne that Operation Ajax saved for Mohammad Reza Shah in 1953 has now fallen twice, and this time nobody restores it.
stops.quote: We shall export our revolution to the whole world. Until the cry "There is no god but Allah" resounds over the whole world, there will be struggle.
stops.quote_source: Statement of 11 February 1979, from Excerpts from Speeches and Messages of Imam Khomeini on the Unity of the Muslims; dating per Dilip Hiro, The Longest War, pp. 32, 108. Wording corrected on verification from 'no god but God'.
suggested_refs: The collapse of the Pahlavi state, 11 February 1979

stops.name: Ahmadabad, his name on the schoolhouse
stops.date_confidence: mohammad_mosaddegh.journey.json dates the renaming 1979-01-01; a post-revolution date is used here and the source file's January is flagged. Canonical pin inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: In the village of Ahmadabad, where Mohammad Mosaddegh lived out his last years under house arrest on the family farm and was buried inside the house itself, the villagers rename the high school built at the grave-house. It becomes Emam Khomeini High School. Khomeini denounces Mosaddegh in public, the nationalist prime minister whose constitutionalism he does not accept and whose secular following he intends to inherit or break. The revolution he leads has ended the monarchy that the 1953 coup against Mosaddegh preserved, and the two names now share one building.
suggested_refs: Emam Khomeini High School at Mosaddegh's grave-house, Ahmadabad

stops.name: Tehran, the referendum with one question
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The question printed on the ballot is Islamic Republic, yes or no. No third form of the state is offered and no alternative appears on the paper. The result announced is ninety-eight percent in favour. Bazargan's provisional government had wanted a wider question and does not get one. The Republic is proclaimed and dated from this day, and what it will be is still unwritten: the draft constitution of the spring says nothing about a supreme jurist, and the assembly that will insert him has not yet been elected.
suggested_refs: The referendum of 30-31 March 1979

stops.name: Kurdistan, the fatwa of jihad
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested. The place is not: the chronology lens gives only 'Kurdistan, Iran' with no coordinates, and this pin is a representative point in the Iranian Kurdish provinces. It is the weakest coordinate in the file.
stops.campa: Kurdish parties in the northwest refuse the new order and take up arms for autonomy. Khomeini issues a fatwa declaring jihad against them, and the young republic fights its first war inside its own frontiers, in provinces where most of the population is Sunni and where the revolution arrived as somebody else's revolution. The state that came to power over the graves at Behesht-e Zahra has existed five months. A radio broadcast from Qom the following day puts the matter to the country without ornament.
stops.quote: Allah did not create man so that he could have fun. The aim of creation was for mankind to be put to the test through hardship and prayer.
stops.quote_source: Radio Iran broadcast from Qom, 20 August 1979, quoted in Amir Taheri, The Spirit of Allah: Khomeini and the Islamic Revolution (1986)
suggested_refs: The fatwa of 19 August 1979 against the Kurdish parties

stops.name: The Temple Mount, the day he instituted
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the interlock lens states plainly that this crossing is not attested in any atlas file and is offered as a reconstructable pin inheritance. The institution of Quds Day is dated to 1979 without a day; the last Friday of Ramadan that year falls in August.
stops.campa: In the first Ramadan of the revolution he institutes a day: on the last Friday of the fast, the Muslim world is to come into the streets for Jerusalem and against the occupation of it. He never sees the city. No Iranian state pilgrimage reaches the esplanade where the Dome stands, and none is planned. The day outlives him. The Republic keeps it every year, in Tehran and wherever it has friends and clients, and the city it is kept for remains a place no Iranian delegation enters.
suggested_refs: Quds Day, instituted 1979, kept annually on the last Friday of Ramadan
sources: Inferred; the interlock lens states no atlas file currently carries this crossing

stops.name: Tehran, the embassy on Taleqani Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Shah's admission to New York on 22 October 1979 is folded into this stop; no separate pin, since Khomeini was not there.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of October the United States admits the Shah to New York for cancer treatment, and Tehran reads the hospital as the rehearsal of 1953. On the fourth of November, the fifteenth anniversary of the day Khomeini was put on a plane to Turkey, students climb the walls of the American embassy and take fifty-two hostages. He did not order it. He endorses it within days and calls the compound a nest of spies, and the hostages are held four hundred and forty-four days. Bazargan resigns and the provisional government ends with him.
suggested_refs: The United States embassy compound, Tehran, seized 4 November 1979

stops.name: Tehran, the office written into law
stops.date_confidence: attested; the chronology lens carries the installation as Supreme Leader and the December constitutional referendum as two entries for substantially one act, and they are given one stop here.
stops.campa: The constitution adopted by referendum in December writes the Najaf lectures into law: an office of Leader standing above the president and the parliament, held by a jurist, with command of the armed forces and the power to remove the elected head of state. Khomeini is named to it for life by the text itself. Nine years earlier this was an argument made to a few dozen students in an Iraqi shrine city. Abolhassan Banisadr is elected first president under the new order in February, and finds out what the office above him is for.
stops.quote: Only one party, and that is party of Allah [Hezbollah], party of the underprivileged.
stops.quote_source: Ruhollah Khomeini, Sahifeh-ye Imam, vol. 9, p. 282, cited on Wikiquote, 'Ruhollah Khomeini'
suggested_refs: The constitution of the Islamic Republic, December 1979, articles on the velayat-e faqih

stops.name: Jamaran, the house in the foothills
stops.date_confidence: the residence runs 1979-1989; 1980 is a placeholder inside it. Coordinates corrected on verification: the geography lens gave 35.8103, 51.4708, about 2 km southeast, and the afterlife lens 35.8171, 51.4405.
stops.campa: He does not live in a palace and does not enter one. He settles in Jamaran, a village swallowed by the northern edge of Tehran under the Alborz, in a small house beside a husseiniya where he receives delegations and speaks to them from behind a window. From these rooms he governs for a decade: rulings, appointments, dismissals, and the arbitration of quarrels between the men who run the ministries. What the Republic decides in the nineteen-eighties is carried up this hill first, to be approved or refused in a plain room.
suggested_refs: The Jamaran house and husseiniya, seat of government 1979-1989

segments.name: The War and the Two Fatwas

stops.name: The southern front, Iraq invades
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; day defaulted to 01. The chronology lens gives the place as 'Iran-Iraq border' with no coordinates; this pin is a representative point on the southern front and is not a sourced location.
stops.campa: Iraqi divisions cross the border on a front of several hundred miles, aiming at Khuzestan and its oil, in the belief that a country which has purged its officer corps and lost its American supply cannot fight. Saddam Hussein, who had Khomeini expelled from Najaf two years earlier, offers terms after the first months. Khomeini refuses them, and refuses every offer that follows, on the ground that the war is now a religious duty and its object is Baghdad. Eight years and several hundred thousand dead proceed from that refusal.
suggested_refs: The Iraqi invasion of September 1980 and the Khuzestan front
sources: QUEUE.md lines 224-225 (Saddam Hussein crossing, queue entry only)

stops.name: Mecca, the pilgrims in the street
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, year only: the interlock lens offers this crossing at the canonical Kaaba pin and states that it is not attested in any atlas file. The month is not given in the pool.
stops.campa: Iranian pilgrims march through Mecca in the demonstration he has made part of the hajj, disavowal of the unbelievers, carrying his portrait through the holy city. Saudi security meets them and more than four hundred people die, most of them Iranian. Riyadh calls it a riot. Tehran calls it a massacre and holds funerals for martyrs killed on pilgrimage. The circuit he is assumed to have made here once, privately, in a year no biographer wrote down, is now an instrument of a state that is at war on two fronts at once.
suggested_refs: The 1987 Mecca incident and the Iranian hajj demonstrations
sources: Inferred; the interlock lens states no atlas file currently carries this crossing

stops.name: Jamaran, the cup of poison
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; day defaulted to 01. The war formally ends in August 1988, also month-only in the pool.
stops.campa: After eight years he accepts the United Nations ceasefire, having sworn for six of them that the war would end in Baghdad and nowhere else. The message is read out for him. He says the decision is more deadly to him than poison, that he drinks the cup for the sake of God, and that he had promised to fight to the last drop of his blood. The war formally ends the following month. He does not apologise for any of it, and puts that in writing to the clergy so that nobody afterward can enter an apology on his behalf.
stops.quote: we do not repent, nor are we sorry for even a single moment for our performance during the war.
stops.quote_source: Khomeini, Letter to Clergy, quoted in Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah (2000), p. 285. Wording corrected on verification from 'our conduct in the war'.
suggested_refs: The July 1988 acceptance of UN Security Council Resolution 598
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Jamaran, the ruling on The Satanic Verses
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of February Radio Tehran broadcasts a ruling issued from the house at Jamaran. The author of The Satanic Verses, together with every editor and publisher aware of its contents, is condemned to death, and Muslims anywhere in the world are called upon to carry the sentence out without delay. Salman Rushdie, a British subject who has broken no law of the country he lives in, goes into hiding. The ruling asserts a jurisdiction that stops at no frontier. Its author has three and a half months to live.
stops.quote: We are from Allah and to Allah we shall return. I am informing all brave Muslims of the world that the author of The Satanic Verses, a text written, edited, and published against Islam, the Prophet of Islam, and the Qur'an, along with all the editors and publishers aware of its contents, are condemned to death. I call on all valiant Muslims wherever they may be in the world to kill them without delay, so that no one will dare insult the sacred beliefs of Muslims henceforth.
stops.quote_source: Fatwa broadcast on Radio Tehran, 14 February 1989; English Wikipedia, 'The Satanic Verses controversy', n. 35
suggested_refs: The Radio Tehran broadcast of 14 February 1989

stops.name: Tehran, the death in the hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested. The age is contested: 89 by the 1900 birth certificate, 86 by the 1902 family date, and both numbers appear in the pool.
stops.campa: He dies in a Tehran hospital after surgery to stop internal bleeding, following years of heart disease and cancer. State radio breaks its programming to announce the death of the Imam. He is eighty-nine by the certificate and eighty-six by the date his family preferred, and both numbers run in the papers of the same week, forty years of dispute about a birth arriving at last at the other end of the life. Ten months earlier he had accepted the ceasefire. Four months earlier he had condemned a novelist. Neither is withdrawn.
suggested_refs: The Tehran hospital where the final surgery was performed

stops.name: Behesht-e Zahra, the torn shroud
stops.date_confidence: attested. Crowd estimates diverge sharply and are not reconciled: roughly two million by some sources, roughly ten million by others.
stops.campa: The body is carried to the cemetery in an open refrigerated coffin above a crowd counted at two million by some and ten million by others. The barriers break. The coffin goes over, the shroud tears, hands pull at the cloth for relics, and the body is very nearly lost in the press of people. The burial is abandoned; a helicopter lifts the body out; the interment is finished hours later under guard, in a sealed container, with the mourners held at a distance. The funeral happens twice in one afternoon, once in the hands of the crowd and once under guard, and the second one is the one that works.
suggested_refs: Wire and broadcast footage of the funeral of 6 June 1989
sources: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Tehran, the succession
stops.date_confidence: the pool dates the succession to June 1989 without a day; 4 June is placed the day after the death, between death and funeral.
stops.campa: Ali Khamenei, the sitting president, is named Leader. He is not a source of emulation, and the doctrine as Khomeini wrote it in Najaf asked for one. The rank the dead man spent sixty years acquiring in the seminary is detached, at the very first succession, from the office that was built to require it. Every subsequent quarrel in Iran about who may rule in the name of the jurist runs back to the week of the funeral, when the question was settled quickly because the alternative to settling it quickly was worse.
suggested_refs: The Assembly of Experts session of June 1989

stops.name: Behesht-e Zahra, the mausoleum over the grave
stops.date_confidence: groundbreaking attested to 19 July 1989. Coordinates corrected on verification: the geography lens gave 35.585, 51.455, about 9 km off. The master plan and the cost criticism are tagged [R] in the pool, with figures reported inconsistently.
stops.campa: Ground is broken six weeks after the burial. What goes up over the grave is not a tomb but a complex: a gold dome, four minarets of ninety-one metres each, and on the master plan a seminary, a university, a convention centre, a hotel, and shopping. It is built to draw pilgrims the way Mashhad draws them. The cost is criticised inside Iran through years of austerity and the figures reported for it do not agree with one another. The cemetery chosen in February 1979 for the revolution's dead becomes the shrine of the man who spoke over them.
suggested_refs: The Mausoleum of Ruhollah Khomeini, ground broken 19 July 1989
sources: Iranian state media (IRNA/Mehr News) on the shrine expansion

stops.name: Tehran, the collected works and the withheld poems
stops.date_confidence: the Sahifeh-ye Imam is compiled through the 1990s; the Divan-e Imam appears in 1989. 1990 is a placeholder for the compilation. The Divan's suppression during his lifetime is tagged [R] in the pool.
stops.campa: An institute is founded to gather everything he wrote and said, speeches, letters, rulings, marginalia, into the Sahifeh-ye Imam, commonly cited at twenty-two volumes and treated as the authoritative text of his positions. In the same years his Persian poetry appears as the Divan-e Imam, withheld through his lifetime by his own decision: ghazals in the Sufi manner, the wine and the tavern and the Beloved, written by the jurist who condemned a novelist. The Republic prints both and does not comment on the distance between them.
stops.quote: Most of the wailings of the awliya [pious believers] is caused by the pain of separation and detachment from the Beloved and His Generosity.
stops.quote_source: Ruhollah Khomeini, Pithy Aphorisms: Wise Saying and Counsels, ed. Mansoor Limba (Tehran: Institute for Compilation and Publication of Imam Khomeini's Works), p. 3. Restored on verification from a truncated submission.
suggested_refs: Sahifeh-ye Imam, Institute edition; Divan-e Imam (1989)
sources: Institute for Compilation and Publication of Imam Khomeini's Works
Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah

stops.name: Jamaran, the museum and the grandson
stops.date_confidence: the disqualification is attested to the 2016 Assembly of Experts election, held 26 February 2016; the pool gives the year only. The anniversary correction is applied: 14 Khordad is 4 June, not mid-June as the afterlife lens had it.
stops.campa: The Jamaran house is kept as a museum by the institute that publishes him: the prayer room, the personal effects, the room where he died. The anniversary of the death is a national holiday, the fourteenth of Khordad, the fourth of June, and the state restages his memory at the shrine every year for whoever is leading it now. His grandson Hassan Khomeini, a mid-ranking cleric, runs the institute and the family foundations. In 2016 the Guardian Council refuses him a place on the ballot for the Assembly of Experts.
suggested_refs: The Jamaran memorial museum; the 2016 Assembly of Experts disqualification
sources: Institute for Compilation and Publication of Imam Khomeini's Works
